content: The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines to protect workers from potential risks associated with manufactured nanomaterials (MNMs). These guidelines emphasize best practices, worker involvement, and the importance of education and training. Best Practices for Classifying MNMs The WHO recommends classifying MNMs into three groups based on their properties: 1. Specific Toxicity Group: This includes MNMs with high dissolution rates that release ions or degrade biologically, as well as those with low dissolution rates but high specific toxicity due to their chemical properties. 2. Respirable Fibers Group: These are rigid, biopersistent, or biodurable fibers that are respirable. They meet specific dimensional criteria, such as a fiber length greater than 5 µm, a diameter less than 3 µm, and an aspect ratio greater than 3. 3. Granular Biopersistent Particles (GBP) Group: These are respirable, granular, and biodurable particles with low dissolution rates and no high specific toxicity. They are also referred to as poorly soluble particles or low-toxicity particles. Grouping MNMs with similar properties is crucial in the absence of comprehensive hazard data for new materials. This approach allows for the transfer of hazard information (bridging or read-across) between materials. A systematic review commissioned by the WHO identified three main mechanisms of MNM toxicity: specific material toxicity, inhalation and biopersistence in the lungs, and fiber structure-mediated effects. Worker Involvement The WHO considers it best practice to involve workers in health and safety discussions. Worker participation is often legally mandated in many countries, as outlined in Article 19 of the International Labour Organization’s (ILO) Occupational Safety and Health Convention (C155). This collaboration between workers and employers enhances the control of health and safety risks. MNMs have unique risk profiles that differ from bulk materials, and safety data sheets (SDS) may not always provide reliable information. Training should cover: Hazards specific to MNMs. The European Union (EU) and organizations like the National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences (USA) and the UK Health and Safety Executive provide training materials that can be adapted to local needs. Assessing Health Hazards of MNMs The WHO recommends assigning hazard classes to all MNMs using the Globally Harmonized System (GHS) of Classification and Labeling of Chemicals. Safety data sheets should be updated with MNM-specific hazard information or indicate gaps in toxicological testing. For respirable fibers and granular biopersistent particles, provisional classification can be based on available data. Common hazard classes for MNMs include: Carcinogenicity. Germ cell mutagenicity. Serious eye damage. Respiratory or skin sensitization. Evidence for these classifications is derived from animal and genotoxicity studies reviewed by the OECD and the International Agency for Research on Cancer (IARC). The quality of evidence ranges from moderate to high. 1. 2. 3. Recommendations for Research and Implementation The WHO emphasizes the need for further research to classify additional MNMs and develop reliable safety data sheets. Conclusion The WHO guidelines provide a structured approach to managing the risks of MNMs in the workplace.
